title: Part 2, Chapter 55
paragraphs: What happened to Sancho on the road, and other things that cannot be surpassed

His long delay with Ricote kept Sancho from reaching the duke's castle that day, though he was within half a league of it when night, somewhat dark and cloudy, overtook him. As it was summer, that did not trouble him much, and he turned off the road meaning to wait for morning; but his bad luck and hard fate so arranged it that, while he was looking for a comfortable spot, he and Dapple fell into a deep, dark hole among some very old ruined buildings. As he fell he commended himself with all his heart to God, convinced he would not stop until he hit the bottom of the bottomless pit. But it didn't turn out that way: at little more than three times a man's height Dapple struck bottom, and Sancho found himself sitting on him without the slightest hurt or scrape. He felt himself all over and held his breath to check whether he was sound or had a hole punched in him somewhere, and finding himself whole and in perfect health he poured out thanks to God our Lord for the mercy shown him, since he had been sure he was broken into a thousand pieces. He also ran his hands along the walls of the pit to see if he could get out without help, but they were quite smooth and offered no hold anywhere, which distressed him terribly — especially when he heard how piteously and mournfully Dapple was bemoaning himself, and no wonder he complained, nor was it bad temper, for in truth he was in a very poor state. "Alas," said Sancho, "what unexpected disasters happen at every turn to those who live in this miserable world! Who would have said that a man who saw himself yesterday seated on a throne, governor of an island, ordering servants and vassals about, would see himself today buried in a pit without a soul to help him, without servant or vassal to come to his rescue? Here we must perish of hunger, my ass and I, if indeed we don't die first, he of his bruises and injuries, and I of grief and sorrow. At any rate I won't be as lucky as my master Don Quixote of La Mancha, when he went down into the cave of that enchanted Montesinos, where he found people who made more fuss over him than if he had been in his own house — they say he came in for a table laid out and a bed ready made. There he saw fair and pleasant visions, but here I expect I'll see toads and adders. Unlucky wretch that I am, what an end my follies and fancies have come to! They'll dig up my bones out of this, when heaven wills that I'm found, picked clean, white and polished, and my good Dapple's with them, and by that, perhaps, it will be discovered who we are, at least by those who have heard that Sancho Panza never parted from his ass, nor his ass from Sancho Panza. Unlucky wretches, I say again, that our hard fate should not let us die in our own country and among our own people, where if there was no remedy for our misfortune, at least there would be someone to grieve over it and to close our eyes as we passed away! O comrade and friend, how badly have I repaid your faithful service! Forgive me, and beg Fortune, as best you can, to deliver us out of this miserable strait we are both in; and I promise to set a crown of laurel on your head, and make you look like a poet laureate, and give you double feeds."

In this strain Sancho bewailed himself, and his ass listened but never answered a word, such was the distress and anguish the poor beast was in. At last, after a night spent in bitter moaning and lamentation, day came, and by its light Sancho saw it was wholly impossible to climb out of that pit without help, and he fell to bemoaning his fate and shouting loudly to find out if anyone was within hearing; but all his shouting was crying in the wilderness, for there was not a soul anywhere nearby to hear him, and at last he gave himself up for dead. Dapple was lying on his back, and Sancho got him to his feet, which he could barely keep; and then taking a piece of bread out of his saddlebags that had shared their fortunes in the fall, he gave it to the ass, who was not at all sorry to have it, and said to him as if he understood, "With bread all sorrows are less."

Then he noticed on one side of the pit a hole large enough to admit a person if he stooped and squeezed himself small. Sancho went over and crept through, and found it wide and spacious inside, which he was able to see because a ray of sunlight that came through what you might call the roof showed it all plainly. He saw too that it opened out and widened into another spacious cavity; so he made his way back to where the ass was, and with a stone began to pick the clay away from the hole until in a short time he had made room for the beast to pass easily. Then taking him by the halter, he set off through the cavern to see if there was any way out at the other end. He advanced, sometimes in the dark, sometimes without light, but never without fear. "God Almighty help me!" he said to himself; "what is a misadventure to me would make a fine adventure for my master Don Quixote. He would have been sure to take these depths and dungeons for flowery gardens or the palaces of Galiana, and would have counted on emerging from this darkness and confinement into some blooming meadow; but I, unlucky as I am, hopeless and dispirited, expect at every step another pit deeper than the first to open under my feet and swallow me up for good — 'welcome evil, if you come alone.'"

In this way and with these reflections he seemed to himself to have travelled a bit more than half a league when at last he made out a faint glimmer that looked like daylight finding its way in on one side, showing that this road, which seemed to him the road to the other world, led to some opening.

Here Cide Hamete leaves him and returns to Don Quixote, who in high spirits and contentment was looking forward to the day set for the battle he was to fight with the man who had robbed Doña Rodriguez's daughter of her honour, for whom he hoped to obtain satisfaction for the wrong and injury so shamefully done her. So it happened that, having ridden out one morning to practise and exercise what he would have to do in the encounter awaiting him the next day, as he was putting Rocinante through his paces or pressing him to the charge, he brought the horse's hooves so close to a pit that, but for reining him in tightly, there would have been no avoiding a fall into it. He pulled him up without going down, and coming a little closer examined the hole without dismounting; but as he was looking at it he heard loud cries coming from below, and by listening carefully was able to make out that whoever was uttering them was saying, "Hey, up there! is there any Christian who hears me, or any charitable gentleman who will take pity on a sinner buried alive, on a disgoverned, unfortunate governor?"

It struck Don Quixote that it was Sancho Panza's voice he heard, at which he was taken aback and astonished, and raising his own voice as much as he could, he called out, "Who is down there? Who is that complaining?"

"Who should be here, or who should complain," came the answer, "but the forlorn Sancho Panza, for his sins and for his bad luck governor of the island of Barataria, squire-that-was to the famous knight Don Quixote of La Mancha?"

When Don Quixote heard this his astonishment was redoubled and his agitation grew greater than ever, for it occurred to him that Sancho must be dead and his soul in torment down there; and carried away by the idea he exclaimed, "I conjure you by everything I as a Catholic Christian can conjure you by, tell me who you are; and if you are a soul in torment, tell me what you would have me do for you, for since my profession is to give aid and succour to those in need in this world, it will extend also to aiding and succouring the distressed of the other world, who cannot help themselves."
"In that case," the voice answered, "your worship who speaks to me must be my master Don Quixote of La Mancha; in fact, from the tone of the voice it is plainly nobody else."

"Don Quixote I am," replied Don Quixote, "he whose profession it is to aid and succour the living and the dead in their needs; therefore tell me who you are, for you are keeping me in suspense — because if you are my squire Sancho Panza, and you are dead, since the devils have not carried you off and by God's mercy you are in purgatory, our holy mother the Roman Catholic Church has intercessory means enough to release you from the pains you are in; and I for my part will plead with her to that end, as far as my resources will allow. Without further delay, then, declare yourself and tell me who you are."

"By all that's good," was the answer, "and by the birth of whomever your worship chooses, I swear, Señor Don Quixote of La Mancha, that I am your squire Sancho Panza, and that I've never died in all my life; but that, having given up my government for reasons that would take more time to explain, I fell last night into this pit where I am now, and Dapple is my witness and won't let me lie about it, because here he is with me, what's more."
And that wasn't all: you would have thought the ass understood what Sancho said, because at that very moment he began to bray so loudly that the whole cave rang.

"Splendid testimony!" exclaimed Don Quixote; "I know that bray as well as if I were its mother, and your voice too, my Sancho. Wait while I go to the duke's castle, which is close by, and I'll bring someone to pull you out of this pit your sins no doubt have landed you in."
"Go, your worship," said Sancho, "and come back quickly, for God's sake; I can't stand being buried alive any longer, and I'm dying of fear."

Don Quixote left him and hurried to the castle to tell the duke and duchess what had happened to Sancho, and they were not a little astonished at it; they could easily understand his having fallen, given the confirming fact of a cave that had been there since time immemorial, but they couldn't imagine how he had quit the government without their getting any notice of his coming. To cut it short, they fetched ropes and tackle, as the saying goes, and by dint of many hands and much labour they hauled Dapple and Sancho Panza out of the darkness into the light of day. A student who saw him remarked, "That's the way all bad governors should come out of their governments, as this sinner comes out of the depths of the pit — dead with hunger, pale, and I'd guess without a penny to his name."

Sancho overheard him and said, "It's eight or ten days, brother growler, since I entered upon the government of the island they gave me, and in all that time I never had a bellyful of food, not even for an hour; doctors persecuted me and enemies crushed my bones; nor had I any chance to take bribes or collect taxes; and if that's the case, as it is, I don't think I deserve to come out in this fashion; but 'man proposes and God disposes'; and God knows what is best, and what suits each one best; and 'as the occasion, so the behaviour'; and 'let nobody say "I won't drink of this water"'; and 'where you think there are bacon flitches, there are no pegs to hang them on'; God knows my meaning and that's enough; I say no more, though I could."

"Don't be angry or annoyed at what you hear, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "or there'll never be an end of it; keep a safe conscience and let them say what they like, for trying to stop slanderers' tongues is like trying to put gates on the open plain. If a governor comes out of his government rich, they say he's been a thief; and if he comes out poor, that he's been a fool and a blockhead."
"They'll be pretty sure this time," said Sancho, "to set me down as a fool rather than a thief."

Talking thus, and surrounded by boys and a crowd of people, they reached the castle, where in one of the corridors the duke and duchess stood waiting for them; but Sancho would not go up to see the duke until he had first stabled Dapple, for he said the poor beast had passed a very bad night in his last quarters. Then he went upstairs to see his lord and lady, and kneeling before them said, "Because it was your highnesses' pleasure, and not from any merit of my own, I went to govern your island of Barataria, which 'I entered naked, and naked I find myself; I neither lose nor gain.' Whether I have governed well or ill, I have had witnesses who will say what they please. I have answered questions, I have decided cases, and always dying of hunger, for Doctor Pedro Recio of Tirteafuera, the island's and governor's doctor, would have it so. Enemies attacked us by night and put us in a great fix, but the people of the island say they came out safe and victorious by the might of my arm — may God give them as much health as there is truth in what they say. In short, during that time I have weighed the cares and responsibilities of governing, and by my reckoning my shoulders can't bear them, nor are they a load for my loins or arrows for my quiver; and so, before the government threw me over, I preferred to throw the government over; and yesterday morning I left the island as I found it, with the same streets, houses, and roofs it had when I came in. I asked no loan of anyone, nor did I try to fill my pocket; and though I meant to make some useful laws, I made hardly any, since I was afraid they wouldn't be kept; for in that case it comes to the same thing to make them or not to make them. I quit the island, as I said, with no escort except my ass; I fell into a pit, I pressed on through it, until this morning by the light of the sun I saw a way out, but not so easy a one but that, had not heaven sent me my master Don Quixote, I'd have stayed there till the end of the world. So now my lord and lady duke and duchess, here is your governor Sancho Panza, who in the bare ten days he has held the government has come by the knowledge that he wouldn't give anything to be governor, not to say of an island, but of the whole world; and that point being settled, kissing your worships' feet, and imitating the game of the boys when they say, 'jump and give me one,' I take a leap out of the government and pass into the service of my master Don Quixote; for after all, though there I eat my bread in fear and trembling, at least I eat my fill; and for my part, so long as I'm full, it's all the same to me whether it's with carrots or with partridges."

Here Sancho brought his long speech to an end, Don Quixote having been the whole time in dread of his uttering a host of absurdities; and when he found him leave off with so few, he gave heartfelt thanks to heaven. The duke embraced Sancho and told him he was heartily sorry he had given up the government so soon, but that he would see to it he was provided with some other post on his estate less burdensome and more profitable. The duchess also embraced him, and gave orders that he should be taken good care of, for it was plain to see he had been badly treated and worse bruised.
